claim: Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, two mainstream guidelines for defining when to end the isolation of SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals have been in use: the one-size-fits-all approach (i.e. patients are isolated for a fixed number of days) and the personalized approach (i.e. based on repeated testing of isolated patients).
source: Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, two mainstream guidelines for defining when to end the isolation of SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals have been in use: the one-size-fits-all approach (i.e. patients are isolated for a fixed number of days) and the personalized approach (i.e. based on repeated testing of isolated patients).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about existing guidelines, supported by the context of the manuscript and general knowledge of COVID-19 policies.

claim: By considering a fixed time of 10 days since symptom onset as the criterion for ending isolation, the risk of releasing an individual who is still infectious is low (0–6.6%).
source: By considering a fixed time of 10 days since symptom onset as the criterion for ending isolation, we estimated that the risk of releasing an individual who is still infectious is low (0–6.6%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript, specifically from the analysis of the one-size-fits-all approach.

claim: A fixed isolation period of 10 days entails lengthy unnecessary isolations (4.8–8.3 days).
source: However, this policy entails lengthy unnecessary isolations (4.8–8.3 days).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results showing the duration of prolonged isolation under the one-size-fits-all approach.

claim: By using a personalized strategy, similar low risks can be reached with shorter prolonged isolations compared to the one-size-fits-all approach.
source: In contrast, by using a personalized strategy, similar low risks can be reached with shorter prolonged isolations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis of the two approaches presented in the manuscript.

claim: The number of COVID-19 cases reached 80 million by the end of 2020.
source: Since the first case of a novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) was identified in China in December of 2019, its associated disease, COVID-19, spread quickly around the world, with the number of cases reaching 80 million by the end of 2020.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the number of COVID-19 cases, which is established knowledge from public health records.

claim: By considering a fixed time of 10 days since symptom onset as the criterion for ending isolation, the probability of releasing patients who are still infectious was estimated to be 0.9% (95%CI: 0.6 to 1.2), with a lengthy prolonged isolation of 6.8 days (95% empirical CI: 1 to 8) when considering 10^5 copies/mL as the infectiousness threshold value.

source: The estimated probability of prematurely ending isolation becomes 6.6% (95%CI: 5.8 to 7.4) and 0% with a prolonged isolation of 4.8 days (95% empirical CI: −2 to 8) and 8.3 days (95% empirical CI: 6 to 10) if we consider 104.5 and 105.5 copies/mL as infectiousness threshold values, respectively (Figure 2A).

claim: The length of the prolonged isolation for a <5% risk was estimated to be 3.8 days (95% empirical CI: −2 to 5), 5.8 days (95% empirical CI: −2 to 8), and 3.3 days (95% empirical CI: 0 to 4) for infectiousness threshold values of 10^5.0, 10^4.5, and 10^5.5 copies/mL, respectively.

claim: By considering two consecutive negative test results repeated at an interval of 1 day as the criterion for ending isolation, the probability of prematurely ending isolation was estimated to be 8.1% (95%CI: 7.2 to 9.0) with a negligible length of prolonged isolation of 1.2 days (95% empirical CI: −1 to 3) when considering 10^5.0 copies/mL as the infectiousness threshold value.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van Kampen et al., 2021; Wölfel et al., 2020.

claim: The uncertainty in the infectiousness threshold is reflected in the high variability in the results obtained for the one-size-fits-all approach.
source: Such uncertainty is reflected in the high variability in the results obtained for the one-size-fits-all approach; on the other hand, the personalized approach provided stable results with respect to the infectiousness threshold values.
evidence: This is an inference about how uncertainty in the threshold affects the two approaches.

claim: The personalized approach provided stable results with respect to the infectiousness threshold values.
source: Such uncertainty is reflected in the high variability in the results obtained for the one-size-fits-all approach; on the other hand, the personalized approach provided stable results with respect to the infectiousness threshold values.
evidence: This is an inference about the robustness of the personalized approach.

claim: Arbitrary values for the risk of prematurely ending isolation (namely, 1% or 5%) were considered.
source: Fourth, we considered arbitrary values for the risk of prematurely ending isolation (namely, 1% or 5%).
evidence: This is a description of a methodological choice in the study.

claim: Whether such risks are acceptable depends on several factors such as the epidemiological context, the aim of the adopted policies, and propensity to take risks.
source: Whether such risks are acceptable depends on several factors such as the epidemiological context (e.g. the prevalence of the infection and disease burden), the aim of the adopted policies (e.g. suppression of transmission, mitigation of disease burden), propensity to take risks.
evidence: This is an inference about the context-dependent nature of risk acceptability.

claim: If for a certain level of risk, the difference between the personalized and one-size-fits-all approaches is small, the fixed duration approach may have the advantage in terms of simplicity, cost, and resources.
source: Nonetheless, it is worth remarking that, if for a certain level of risk, the difference between the personalized and one-size-fits-all approaches is small, the fixed duration approach may have the advantage in terms of simplicity, cost, and resources.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical trade-offs between the two approaches.

claim: In the personalized approach, qualitative PCR test results only (i.e. whether the viral load is above or below a given threshold) were used.
source: We also note that in the personalized approach, we used qualitative PCR test results only (i.e. whether the viral load is above or below a given threshold).
evidence: This is a description of a methodological choice in the study.

claim: The use of quantitative PCR test results may enable prediction of the optimal day to end isolation for each patient.
source: The use of quantitative PCR test results may enable us to predict the optimal day to end isolation for each patient.
evidence: This is speculation about potential improvements to the personalized approach.

claim: The timing of the first test does not influence much the findings, as this analysis primarily focuses on the time when the viral load crosses the infectiousness threshold.
source: As this analysis primarily focuses on the time when the viral load crosses the infectiousness threshold, we do not expect that the timing of the first test does not influence much our findings.
evidence: This is an inference about the robustness of the findings to the timing of testing.

claim: Starting the tests too early since isolation (or symptom onset) might be impractical and it should be determined based on operational and cost constraints.
source: However, starting the tests too early since isolation (or symptom onset) might be impractical and it should be determined based on operational and cost constraints.
evidence: This is an inference about practical considerations for implementing the personalized approach.

claim: The guidelines regulating the length of isolation of COVID-19 patients require further updating following new epidemiologic and clinical knowledge, patient characteristics, and the capability of health sectors.
source: The guidelines regulating the length of isolation of COVID-19 patients require further updating following new epidemiologic and clinical knowledge, patient characteristics, and the capability of health sectors, such as test availability.
evidence: This is an inference about the need for ongoing updates to guidelines.

claim: In several countries, isolation guidelines have been updated several times throughout the course of the pandemic.
source: Indeed, in several countries, these guidelines have been updated several times throughout the course of the pandemic (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2020a; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2020a; Public Health England, 2020) and the emergence of new variants can spark new adjustments in the future as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2020a; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2020a; Public Health England, 2020.

claim: The emergence of new variants can spark new adjustments to isolation guidelines in the future.
source: Indeed, in several countries, these guidelines have been updated several times throughout the course of the pandemic (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2020a; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2020a; Public Health England, 2020) and the emergence of new variants can spark new adjustments in the future as well.
evidence: This is speculation about future developments.

claim: The proposed modeling framework is very flexible and could be easily adapted to simulate the immune response and effect of antiviral therapies as well as to the study of other infectious diseases.
source: Our proposed modeling framework is very flexible and could be easily adapted to simulate the immune response and effect of antiviral therapies as well as to the study of other infectious diseases.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the modeling framework.

claim: The modeling framework might prove quite relevant should new SARS-CoV-2 variants show different temporal infectiousness profiles than the historical lineage.
source: In particular, it might prove quite relevant should new SARS-CoV-2 variants show different temporal infectiousness profiles than the historical lineage (Davies et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2021 and represents speculation about future applications.

claim: Until the vaccination effort successfully suppresses the widespread circulation of SARS-CoV-2, nonpharmaceutical interventions, and patient isolation in particular, will continue to be a primary tool for mitigating SARS-CoV-2 spread.
source: In conclusion, until the vaccination effort successfully suppresses the widespread circulation of SARS-CoV-2, nonpharmaceutical interventions, and patient isolation in particular, will continue to be a primary tool for mitigating SARS-CoV-2 spread.
evidence: This is an inference about the continued importance of NPIs.

claim: The study used de-identified secondary data from published studies, and thus ethics approval for this study was not necessary.
source: We used the de-identified secondary data from published studies, and thus ethics approval for this study was not necessary.
evidence: This is a description of the ethical considerations for the study.

claim: A mathematical model of SARS-CoV-2 viral dynamics was developed.
source: We developed a mathematical model of SARS-CoV-2 viral dynamics (Ikeda et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2020b; Perelson, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ikeda et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2020b; Perelson, 2002.

claim: Model parameters were calibrated by fitting the longitudinal data with a mixed-effect model.
source: Model parameters were calibrated by fitting the longitudinal data with a mixed-effect model.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: The baseline model is one of the simplest models for viruses causing acute respiratory infection.
source: The model used here (baseline model) is one of the simplest models for viruses causing acute respiratory infection.
evidence: This is a description of the model choice.

claim: Using a simple model represents an appropriate baseline choice given that the biological infection process has not been fully understood yet.
source: Given that the biological infection process has not been fully understood yet, we believe using a simple model represents an appropriate baseline choice.
evidence: This is an inference about the appropriateness of the model choice.

claim: Several different models have been used in the literature of SARS-CoV-2 studies including the baseline model.
source: Specifically in the literature of SAS-CoV-2 studies, several different models have been used including the baseline model (Gonçalves et al., 2020; Goyal et al., 2020; Goyal et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gonçalves et al., 2020; Goyal et al., 2020; Goyal et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2020b.

claim: Two alternative models were considered: the 'eclipse phase' model and the 'innate immune response' model.
source: Nonetheless, to investigate to what extent the model choice affects our findings, we considered two alternative models: the 'eclipse phase' model (Baccam et al., 2006; Gonçalves et al., 2020) and the 'innate immune response' model (Baccam et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baccam et al., 2006; Gonçalves et al., 2020.

claim: In the one-size-fits-all approach, isolation was assumed to end after a fixed time since symptom onset.
source: In the one-size-fits-all approach, we assumed isolation to end after a fixed time since symptom onset, whereas in the personalized approach using PCR tests, isolation ends after obtaining a given number of consecutive negative test results (with a given time interval between the tests).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: In the personalized approach using PCR tests, isolation ends after obtaining a given number of consecutive negative test results (with a given time interval between the tests).
source: In the one-size-fits-all approach, we assumed isolation to end after a fixed time since symptom onset, whereas in the personalized approach using PCR tests, isolation ends after obtaining a given number of consecutive negative test results (with a given time interval between the tests).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: As the baseline scenario for the one-size-fits-all approach, a fixed time of 10 days was considered.
source: As the baseline scenario for the one-size-fits-all approach (here referred to as the 'symptom-based strategy'), we considered a fixed time of 10 days.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: As the baseline scenario for the personalized approach, two consecutive negative test results repeated at a daily interval were considered.
source: As the baseline scenario for the personalized approach (here referred to as the 'test-based strategy'), we considered two consecutive negative test results repeated at a daily interval (in agreement with the CDC guidelines [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2020a]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2020a.

claim: Testing was assumed to start immediately after symptom onset.
source: Here, we assumed the testing starts immediately after symptom onset.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: Epidemiological studies based on contact tracing data suggest that infectiousness nearly disappears 8 days after symptom onset.
source: Epidemiological studies based on contact tracing data suggest that infectiousness nearly disappears 8 days after symptom onset (Hu et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021.

claim: According to Kim et al., 2020b, the 97.5 percentile of the viral load 8 days after symptom onset is 10^5.0 copies/mL.
source: According, to Kim et al., 2020b, the 97.5 percentile of the viral load 8 days after symptom onset is 105.0 copies/mL (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2020b and Kim et al., 2021.

claim: 10^5.0 copies/mL was used as threshold to define whether a patient is still infectious.
source: We thus use 105.0 copies/mL as threshold to define whether a patient is still infectious (i.e. able to transmit the infection).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: Two metrics were computed to evaluate the different strategies: the probability of prematurely ending isolation and the length of unnecessarily prolonged isolation.
source: To evaluate the different strategies, we computed two metrics based on the simulated viral loads: the probability of prematurely ending isolation and the length of unnecessarily prolonged isolation.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: The probability of prematurely ending isolation is the chance that infected patients are released from isolation while they are still infectious.
source: The probability of prematurely ending isolation is the chance that infected patients are released from isolation while they are still infectious.
evidence: This is a definition of one of the metrics used in the study.

claim: The length of prolonged isolation is defined as the difference between the time at which a patient is no longer infectious and the time when her or his isolation ends.
source: The length of prolonged isolation is defined as the difference between the time at which a patient is no longer infectious and the time when her or his isolation ends.
evidence: This is a definition of one of the metrics used in the study.

claim: When the prolonged isolation is negative, it means that the isolation period has ended when the patient is still infectious.
source: Note that when the prolonged isolation is negative, it means that the isolation period has ended when the patient is still infectious.
evidence: This is an explanation of how to interpret the metric.

claim: As sensitivity analyses, the length of isolation in the range of 2 to 20 days was considered for the one-size-fits-all approach.
source: As sensitivity analyses, we considered the length of isolation in the range of 2 to 20 days for the one-size-fits-all approach.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: For the personalized approach, the frequency of testing was considered to vary between 1 and 5 days and the number of consecutive negative test results to vary between 1 and 5.
source: For the personalized approach, the frequency of testing (i.e. the interval between consecutive tests) was considered to vary between 1 and 5 days and the number of consecutive negative test results to vary between 1 and 5.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.
